name: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (1948)
teaser: George Gamow's student Ralph Alpher worked out what the first three minutes of the universe should have produced — mostly hydrogen and helium, in a precise ratio. When astronomers measured the real ratio in the 1960s, it matched to two decimal places. The universe's recipe book had been opened.

exploreAction.targetName: The Alpher-Bethe-Gamow paper (1948)
exploreAction.instruction: Read the famous 'αβγ paper' — Gamow added Hans Bethe's name just so the byline would read alpha-beta-gamma. The physics: in the first minutes, the universe fused protons and neutrons into helium. The prediction of 25% helium by mass matched observations decades later.

name: Hubble's Law (1929)
teaser: Edwin Hubble measured galaxies and found they're all rushing away — and the farther they are, the faster they go. The universe isn't static; it's expanding. This one relationship, v = H₀d, is the foundation of modern cosmology and the reason we know there was a beginning.

exploreAction.targetName: Hubble's 1929 paper on the velocity-distance relation
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Hubble combined redshifts from Vesto Slipher with his own distance measurements to draw the line that became the law. He was using a 100-inch telescope and a slide rule. Every 'expanding universe' headline since traces to this graph.

name: General Relativity (1915)
teaser: Einstein's masterpiece: gravity isn't a force pulling objects together — it's the bending of spacetime itself. Planets orbit because they follow the curves that mass makes in the fabric of the universe. When a 1919 eclipse showed starlight bending exactly as he predicted, Einstein became the most famous scientist alive.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1919 Eddington eclipse expedition results
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Arthur Eddington sailed to Príncipe Island to photograph a total eclipse, measuring whether the Sun bent starlight by the tiny amount Einstein predicted. It did. The result made front pages worldwide and turned a theory into the law of the universe.

name: Gravitational Lensing (1919)
teaser: A direct consequence of general relativity: massive objects bend light like lenses. A galaxy between us and a quasar can bend its light into multiple images, arcs, or complete rings — Einstein rings. The first lens was found in 1979, and lensing now maps dark matter by how it warps the sky.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1979 discovery of the twin quasar Q0957+561
exploreAction.instruction: Read how two 'twin' quasars turned out to be one quasar seen twice through a gravitational lens. Then look at modern lensing surveys — the arcs and rings in Hubble images are curved spacetime, photographed. Gravity as optics.

name: Dark Matter (1933)
teaser: Fritz Zwicky measured the Coma cluster of galaxies and found they move as if held by far more mass than the visible stars can provide — about 90% of the cluster's mass was invisible. He called it 'dark matter.' The universe, it turns out, is mostly made of stuff we can't see.

exploreAction.targetName: Zwicky's 1933 paper on the Coma cluster
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Zwicky applied the virial theorem to galaxy velocities and got a mass far beyond the visible light. He was ridiculed for decades; galaxy rotation curves in the 1970s proved him right. We still don't know what dark matter is — but we know it's there, everywhere.

name: Earliest Galaxies (2022)
teaser: Webb telescope observations in 2022–23 kept pushing the record earlier: galaxies shining when the universe was under 300 million years old — impossibly soon after the Big Bang, some cosmologists said. Some candidates appear too massive and too mature for that early date, forcing a rethink of how galaxies form.

exploreAction.targetName: The JWST early-galaxy candidates and the debate
exploreAction.instruction: Read about galaxies like GLASS-z13, seen at redshift ~13, when the universe was 300 million years old. The debate — some say they're too bright and formed too fast — is live science. You're reading the moment the timeline of the early universe got revised.

name: Quasars (1963)
teaser: In 1963, Maarten Schmidt decoded the mystery of 'radio stars' — objects so bright and so far away that the only explanation was supermassive black holes devouring matter at the centers of galaxies, shining with the light of a trillion suns. The universe got violent overnight.

exploreAction.targetName: Schmidt's 1963 paper identifying quasar 3C 273
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Schmidt realized the odd emission lines of 3C 273 were hydrogen lines shifted red by 16% — meaning the object was billions of light-years away yet still visible. The discovery of quasars revealed the engines at the hearts of galaxies: feeding black holes.

name: Neutron Stars & Pulsars (1967)
teaser: Jocelyn Bell Burnell found a strange signal — a steady pulse every 1.3 seconds — so regular her team half-jokingly called it 'LGM-1' (Little Green Men). It was a pulsar: a collapsed star the size of a city, spinning 600 times a second, sweeping a lighthouse beam of radio waves across Earth.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1967 discovery of the first pulsar
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Bell spotted the pulse in miles of chart paper, ruling out every terrestrial source before concluding it was a star. The 1974 Nobel went to her supervisor, not to her — a famous injustice she handled with grace. A teaspoon of neutron star weighs a billion tons.

name: Stellar Evolution Timeline (1910s-20s)
teaser: By studying star clusters, astronomers discovered that stars are born, age, and die on a schedule set by their mass: massive stars burn fast and die young; small ones smolder for trillions of years. The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, a simple scatter plot of brightness vs. temperature, became the periodic table of stars.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram explained
exploreAction.instruction: Read how plotting stars by luminosity and color reveals the main sequence — where stars spend their lives — plus red giants and white dwarfs. Then read how star clusters are living timelines: all stars in a cluster are the same age, so you watch evolution at a glance.

name: White Dwarfs (1915–30)
teaser: Sirius B, a faint companion to the brightest star in the sky, turned out to be a star the size of Earth with the mass of the Sun — the first white dwarf, discovered from a wobble in Sirius's motion. Its density was so absurd that physicists had to invent quantum degeneracy pressure to explain it.

exploreAction.targetName: The story of Sirius B and the discovery of degenerate matter
exploreAction.instruction: Read how astronomers predicted Sirius B from orbit wobbles before anyone saw it, then measured its light — gravitationally redshifted exactly as relativity predicted. A star that's 200,000 times denser than water: the ghost of a star, packed by gravity into a diamond the size of a planet.

name: Cosmic Redshift (1912)
teaser: Vesto Slipher, an observatory night assistant, measured the spectra of spiral nebulae and found almost all of them shifted toward the red — moving away from us, some at enormous speeds. His 1912 measurements were the raw data that made Hubble's expansion law possible.

exploreAction.targetName: Slipher's pioneering redshift measurements
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Slipher worked with a spectrograph on long exposures — a single spectrum could take nights to capture. His redshifts were so large that the great minds of the day assumed the galaxies were just nearby objects with odd spectra. He was seeing the expansion of the universe and didn't yet know it.

name: The Earth's Core (1906)
teaser: Inge Lehmann, a Danish seismologist, studied earthquake waves that passed through the planet and found they did something impossible — unless the Earth's center was a solid ball inside a liquid one. The inner core, discovered from data alone, is a sphere of iron as hot as the Sun's surface.

exploreAction.targetName: Lehmann's 1936 paper on the inner core
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Lehmann used P-waves that appeared where they shouldn't — the shadow zone — to deduce a solid inner core within the liquid outer core. She was a woman in a field of men, working with pen, paper, and earthquakes. Her 'Lehmann discontinuity' is now a standard chapter in geology.

name: Mid-Ocean Ridges (1950s)
teaser: Sonar mapping of the ocean floor after WWII revealed an 80,000-kilometer chain of underwater mountains — the longest mountain range on Earth — running through every ocean. The discovery that the seafloor splits and spreads from these ridges became the proof that powers plate tectonics.

exploreAction.targetName: Marie Tharp's first map of the ocean floor
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Tharp, a woman barred from ships, drew the ocean floor from echo-sounding data in a New York office — and saw the rift valley down the middle of the Atlantic that her male colleagues initially dismissed as 'girl talk.' Her map showed the continents really had been joined.

name: Seafloor Spreading (1960)
teaser: Harry Hess proposed that the ocean floor spreads outward from mid-ocean ridges like a conveyor belt, carrying continents with it — and the magnetic stripes frozen in the basalt, discovered by Vine and Matthews, proved it. The Earth's surface, it turned out, is recycled on a cycle of 200 million years.

exploreAction.targetName: Hess's 1962 'History of Ocean Basins' paper
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Hess, a naval officer who'd mapped the ocean floor during the war, proposed that new seafloor forms at ridges and sinks at trenches. Then the magnetic stripes: Earth's field has flipped repeatedly, and the seafloor records the flips like a tape recorder. The tape proves the spreading.

name: Meteorite Impacts on Earth (1960s)
teaser: Eugene Shoemaker proved that the Moon's craters were impacts, not volcanoes — then turned that trained eye on Earth and found impact craters hiding everywhere, including under a farm field in Arizona. The idea that space regularly bombs the Earth went from joke to textbook in one career.

exploreAction.targetName: Shoemaker's work on the Barringer Crater
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Shoemaker studied the Arizona crater and the nuclear-test physics of cratering to prove an impact origin. Then follow his legacy: the impact hypothesis for the dinosaurs' extinction, accepted in 1980. The man who started as the Moon's geologist ended up explaining mass death from space.

name: Ice Age Cycles (1837–1940s)
teaser: Louis Agassiz convinced the world that glaciers once covered Europe — the Ice Age. A century later, Milutin Milankovitch calculated that slight wobbles in Earth's orbit and tilt drive the glacial cycles, like a celestial metronome. Core samples from ocean floors and ice sheets proved the rhythm: ice ages every ~100,000 years.

exploreAction.targetName: Milankovitch cycles and the ice-core record
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Agassiz recognized glacial scratches in the Alps, then how Milankovitch computed the orbital wobbles by hand over 30 years. Then the payoff: 1970s ocean cores showed climate oscillating exactly on Milankovitch's periods. The ice ages came in waves, and the waves are orbital.

name: Volcanic Hotspots (1963)
teaser: J. Tuzo Wilson asked why Hawaii's volcanoes line up like beads on a string — and answered that a plume of hot rock rises from deep in the mantle while the Pacific plate drifts over it, stamping out one volcano after another. Hotspots explained chains of islands, and pointed straight at plate tectonics.

exploreAction.targetName: Wilson's 1963 hotspot paper
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Wilson used the ages of Hawaiian volcanoes — progressively older away from the Big Island — to infer a stationary plume and a moving plate. Then the punchline: Yellowstone sits over a hotspot now under the Idaho plains; it will one day be another island in a long chain.

name: Birds Are Dinosaurs (1861–1996)
teaser: It started with Archaeopteryx, a fossil with feathers and teeth, found two years after Darwin published. It ended with feathered dinosaurs from China, including small raptors with true wings. The discovery that birds are living dinosaurs — a branch that survived the asteroid — is now the consensus of paleontology.

exploreAction.targetName: The feathered dinosaur discoveries from Liaoning, China
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Liaoning fossils — dinosaurs preserved with feathers, nesting behavior, and even colors — sealed the bird-dinosaur link. Then look at a chicken's skeleton and a velociraptor's: the same hips, the same wishbone, the same hollow bones. Your lunch is a dinosaur.

name: Tyrannosaurus Rex (1905)
teaser: Barnum Brown found the first Tyrannosaurus skeleton in Montana in 1902; Henry Fairfield Osborn named it 'tyrant lizard king' in 1905. A century of discoveries — including the famous 'Sue' — has revealed T. rex as a powerful predator that may have had feathers as a juvenile and couldn't actually run very fast.

exploreAction.targetName: The discovery story of T. rex and Sue
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Brown found the first partial skeleton — it took crews years to excavate — and how modern work on bite force, bone growth, and feathers has redrawn the king. Sue, the most complete specimen, shows injuries from a lifetime of violence. The king had a hard life.

name: Deep-Sea Hydrothermal Vents (1977)
teaser: A tiny submersible, Alvin, dove to the Galápagos Rift and found hot springs on the seafloor teeming with life — giant tube worms, blind shrimp, clams — living on chemicals, not sunlight. It was the first ecosystem ever found that runs on chemosynthesis, and it rewrote the rules of where life can exist.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1977 discovery of hydrothermal vent communities
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the crew of Alvin saw the tube worms first — red plumes waving in the blackness — and how biologists realized the whole food chain ran on bacteria that eat hydrogen sulfide. Life, powered by the Earth's own heat, in total darkness. The search for alien life expanded to include 'life without sun.'

name: Extremophiles (1960s-70s)
teaser: Scientists found microbes living in boiling hot springs, acid pools, Antarctic ice, and even inside nuclear reactors — organisms that thrive where nothing should live. The discovery of extremophiles changed the definition of 'habitable' and made astrobiologists wonder if Mars, Europa, or Enceladus could harbor life.

exploreAction.targetName: Brock's discovery of Thermus aquaticus in Yellowstone
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Brock found bacteria in Yellowstone's boiling springs — including Thermus aquaticus, whose heat-proof enzyme (Taq polymerase) later powered PCR and the entire DNA revolution. The discovery that life loves extremes gave us both a new biology and the tool that reads our genomes.
